children: BlackRock has sold $71.78 million worth of Bitcoin, according to a widely shared post on X. That number sounds dramatic when you attach the name of the world's largest asset manager to it.

The reality is more mundane, and arguably more telling. The selling traces back to investors pulling money out of BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT), not to Larry Fink's team deciding Bitcoin had a bad vibe.
IBIT is the largest US spot Bitcoin ETF, holding tens of billions of dollars in assets. When shareholders redeem, the fund sells some of the Bitcoin backing those shares to pay them out.

BlackRock has made that point itself. The firm maintains its Bitcoin sales are purely reactive, driven by client demand, and no proprietary Bitcoin selling by BlackRock has been documented. Every sale on record ties back to redemptions.
The $71.78 million figure lands amid a run of similar moves. Research covering mid-October 2026 shows IBIT clients sold approximately $65.4 million in Bitcoin on October 13, 2026.
That followed a much rougher session earlier in the month. On October 7, 2026, IBIT saw $207.7 million in outflows in a single day.
IBIT was not alone that day. Net outflows across all US spot Bitcoin ETFs hit $484.9 million on October 7, which means BlackRock's fund accounted for a sizable slice of the exodus.

Zoom out to the full week, and the picture gets bleaker. Combined outflows from Bitcoin and Ethereum ETF products exceeded $1.2 billion, marking the weakest stretch for these funds since late June 2026.
Bitcoin has been trading in a range of roughly $80,000 to $83,000 during this period. The redemptions have coincided with price swings around that band.
Higher rates matter here for a simple reason. When safe assets start paying more, the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like Bitcoin goes up.
Since launching in January 2024, IBIT has become the default on-ramp for institutions that want Bitcoin exposure without touching a private key.

There is also precedent for large holders trimming positions. Harvard Management reduced its IBIT stake by about $72 million in the fourth quarter of 2025, another case where the selling started with the client, not the issuer.
Framing these flows as "BlackRock sells Bitcoin" makes for a punchy post. It also implies a strategic call by the firm, which the evidence does not support.
BlackRock is acting as a pass-through here. The Bitcoin it sells belongs, functionally, to IBIT shareholders who decided they wanted dollars instead.
What the data actually shows is a sentiment problem among the fund's clients. And for anyone tracking Bitcoin's price, client sentiment may matter more than BlackRock's corporate opinion anyway.

ETF flows have become one of the clearest real-time windows into institutional appetite for Bitcoin. When money pours in, funds buy. When it pours out, they sell, and that selling hits the spot market.

Still, flow data is noisy. One heavy day, like the $207.7 million IBIT saw on October 7, can be followed by smaller outflows or even inflows once markets settle. The October 13 figure of approximately $65.4 million was meaningfully smaller than that early-month spike.
For BlackRock, the stakes are reputational as much as financial. Its insistence that it only follows client demand is part of what makes IBIT credible to cautious institutions.

title: BlackRock sells $71.78 million in Bitcoin as ETF redemptions pile up
